rv.q: Even if Williams's script ends up more as position paper than play, the writer-director, aided by a crack cast, has come up with an efficient delivery system for words that need to be said and heard.
As directed by Markus Potter, this is a fast-paced, clever and funny comedy with an important message.
A deft mixture of comedy and drama? A look at Southern politics pitched nimbly between affection and satire? A little something to think about on the way home? Check, check, and check.
Caught between sitcom gagging and deadly serious matters, Church & State ends up a little bit stranded.
Like most political plays, Jason Odell Williams' Church and State is relevant, often riveting and ultimately not particularly good theater.
Church & State offers an immersion in its chosen subjects of faith and firearms that is about as deep as a child's wading pool.
This play is definitely on my list for one of the best plays of the year.
Church and State packs surprising philosophical punch, though dressed as a comedy.
Jason Odell Williams’s play Church & State, fittingly billed as a serious comedy, hits the mark.
Playwright Jason Odell Williams sends a powerful message, one that resonates long after the play ends.

Under Markus Potter’s even direction, “Church & State” is a worthy examination of the values needed to be in the service of the public in America at this pivotal point in its history and the play raises several significant enduring questions deserving answers.
Church & State is a bang-on jolt that is needed in this world.
The script treads on very familiar ground, and its author would be hard-pressed to find a theater-goer in New York who doesn’t already agree with its obvious message.

Church and State is the political equivalent of fan fiction, in which audience members (presumably left leaning) get to indulge a scenario that feels perfectly logical, and which, ideally, would bring a reasonable resolution to an incredibly complex and divisive issue.
Director Markus Potter creates a nice balance between humor and serious material and keeps the audience engaged for the short 75-minute production.

cn.t: Williams' timely political dramedy about a senator's crisis over guns and faith earns praise for its wit and relevance, though critics split on whether it succeeds as theater or merely preaches to the converted.
